passages.t: ‘Into Your hands I commit my spirit’, and ‘My times are in Your hands’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). He begins in trust: “In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame” (verse 1). Then come the words Jesus would pray: “Into Your hands I commit my spirit; You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth” (verse 5).

The middle of the psalm goes down into misery. “my eyes fail from sorrow, my soul and body as well” (verse 9). “I am forgotten like a dead man, out of mind. I am like a broken vessel” (verse 12). “For I hear the slander of many; there is terror on every side” (verse 13).

Then he turns again. “But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, ‘You are my God.’” (verse 14). “My times are in Your hands” (verse 15). He remembers his fear and God's answer: “In my alarm I said, ‘I am cut off from Your sight!’ But You heard my plea for mercy” (verse 22).

It ends speaking to everyone listening: “Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
This psalm swings between trust and trouble more than once. That is how real prayer often goes.

‘Into Your hands I commit my spirit’ is the language of handing something over for safekeeping, like leaving a valuable thing with someone you trust. ‘Spirit’ here means life, breath. He gives his life into God's keeping.

‘A broken vessel’ (verse 12) is a cracked clay pot, thrown away because it is useless. Clay pots were cheap and common. He feels thrown out with the rubbish.

‘Terror on every side’ (verse 13) is also the cry of the prophet Jeremiah's enemies about him (Jeremiah 20:10).

‘My times are in Your hands’ (verse 15) means every part of his life, its seasons and its end, belongs to God, not to his enemies.
passages.later:
As he died on the cross, “Jesus called out in a loud voice, ‘Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.’” (Luke 23:46). The book page notes that Luke records this last word from Psalm 31:5, as Matthew and Mark record the cry from Psalm 22. Jesus added one word, ‘Father’.

Stephen, the first Christian martyr, prayed in the same spirit as he died: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). Peter tells believers who suffer to “entrust their souls to their faithful Creator” (1 Peter 4:19).
passages.hard: Verse 10 says, ‘my iniquity has drained my strength.’ Does that mean his suffering was a punishment for sin? The psalm does not explain it that way. He sees his sin, and he sees his suffering, and he brings both to God. The notes on Psalms 32 and 38 say more about sin and sickness.
passages.asks:
Verse 5 is a prayer for the end of a day, and for the end of a life. You can say it tonight before you sleep: into your hands I commit my spirit.

And verse 15 is for days when life feels out of control. Say it slowly: ‘My times are in Your hands.’ Not in your boss's, your doctor's, or your enemy's.
